analysis.one_liner: Cancels federal contracts and bans repeat violators of the Davis-Bacon wage law for ten years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees in February 1999 and died when that Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal construction contractors must already pay workers the locally 'prevailing' wage under the Davis-Bacon Act. This bill would have strengthened that law two ways: a contractor found to have a pattern of violating it would lose its federal contract and be barred from new federal contracts for ten years, unless it proved the violations were honest mistakes. It also would have made employee names and addresses in contractors' payroll records available for public inspection, so compliance could actually be audited.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers on federally funded projects, who would gain a real enforcement tool against contractors that shortchange their wages, plus watchdogs and unions that could inspect payroll records to check compliance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal construction workers and wage-law watchdogs

how_it_helps.text: A contractor with a pattern of Davis-Bacon violations would automatically lose its federal contract and be ineligible for federal contracts for ten years, unless it showed the violations were unintentional 'simple and unsystematic error' [S2][S3].
Payroll records — including employee names and addresses — under Davis-Bacon contracts would have to be disclosed for compliance audits, overriding existing privacy-law exemptions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal construction contractors that underpay workers would face contract cancellation, a ten-year federal debarment, and public scrutiny of their payroll records; compliant contractors face new disclosure burdens but no penalty.

drawbacks.text: The mandatory ten-year debarment triggers on a 'pattern of violations' with the burden on the contractor to prove innocent error; critics of rigid debarment laws argue this can sweep in sloppy paperwork as well as deliberate wage cheating [S3].
Releasing employee names and addresses from payroll records overrides privacy protections and exposes workers' personal information to anyone requesting it in connection with an audit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The enforcement teeth are real but blunt: automatic contract cancellation plus a ten-year ban is a strong deterrent against wage theft, and payroll transparency is the only way violations get detected at all. The honest cost is that a strict liability-plus-debarment design could penalize contractors for recordkeeping mistakes, and the payroll disclosure exposes workers' personal data. On balance the bill's benefits — protecting wages the government has already promised to pay — outweigh these costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, then to their subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill on February 3, 1999 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the Committees on Education and the Workforce and on Government Reform [S5].
In late February 1999 it was referred to subcommittees — Government Management, Information and Technology (Feb 17) and Workforce Protections (Feb 26) — where no further action was taken [S5].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died without any committee vote or floor action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors that shortchange workers' prevailing wages keep operating with no threat of debarment, and their payroll records stay shielded from public inspection. The bill's death costs nothing to anyone else — it simply leaves workers without an enforcement tool they never had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contractors that underpay federal construction workers

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Davis-Bacon Enforcement Act of 1999 on February 3, 1999

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of primary referral; its Workforce Protections Subcommittee held the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred to the Workforce Protections Subcommittee on February 26, 1999; no hearing or markup was ever held

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support or opposition is recorded.

industries.note: The bill would cancel their contracts and bar them from federal work for ten years if they establish a pattern of underpaying Davis-Bacon wages, and would open their payroll records to audit. Because these contractors gain by paying less than the legally required prevailing wage, their interest runs against the workers' paychecks.

industries.industry: Government contract compliance and FOIA watchdogs
industries.note: Payroll names and addresses from Davis-Bacon contracts would become inspectable for audits, giving unions, auditors, and watchdogs the data needed to detect violations.
